title: What If You Were Born as Hassan-i Sabbah? | The Order of Assassins

paras: If you were born as Hassan-i Sabbah, you'd take a mountain fortress without fighting a single battle.
You'd live inside it for thirty-four years. And never once come down.
And your own two sons?
You'll have them both executed.
But right now?
You're a baby in the city of Qom, in Persia.
No fortress. No followers. Not even the word assassin. That word doesn't exist yet.
It's the ten-fifties. Nobody wrote down the exact year.
Your father is Ali, a man from Kufa in Iraq.
He says the family goes back to the old kings of Yemen.
Everyone says that. He might even be right.
The family moves to Rey, a big city near where Tehran stands today.
You're raised a Twelver Shia, and you study like it's a sport.
Religion. Law. Anything with pages.
Remember the books.
Then a man named Amira Zarrab starts talking to you.
He's an Ismaili. A different branch of Shia Islam.
His people follow a living imam, the Fatimid caliph, far away in Cairo.
You argue with him. Again and again.
You're sure you're winning.
Then you fall sick. Badly sick. The kind of fever people don't walk away from.
Remember the fever.
You live.
And when you get up, you're not the same boy.
At about seventeen, you swear an oath to the caliph in Cairo.
One fever, and the whole future of Persia tilts.
In 1072, the head of the Ismaili mission in Persia notices you.
His name is Abd al-Malik ibn Attash.
He gives you a job inside the secret network.
Your new title is dai. A summoner. A recruiter of souls.
Persia belongs to the Seljuk Turks now.
They're Sunni, they're powerful, and they hate your movement.
So everything happens quietly. Houses. Whispers. Coded words.
You learn to wait. Remember that.
In 1078 you finally reach Egypt.
Cairo. The capital of the imam you swore your life to.
It's the biggest city you've ever seen.
You stay about three years, in Cairo and Alexandria.
But the real power there isn't the caliph.
It's his army chief and vizier, Badr al-Jamali.
And Badr does not like you.
The chronicles say you clash. Nobody agrees on exactly why.
Some say you backed the wrong son as the next imam.
Either way, Badr has you thrown out of Egypt.
Remember Cairo.
In 1081 you're back in Isfahan with nothing but a plan.
For nine years, you walk.
Across deserts, villages, mountain passes.
Preaching in kitchens. Recruiting in markets.
You're looking for something specific.
Not a city. Cities can be surrounded.
You want a rock that no army can climb.
And around 1087 you find it.
In the Alborz mountains, about a hundred kilometres from Qazvin.
A narrow ridge of stone, more than two thousand metres up.
On top sits a castle called Alamut.
The name is usually linked to eagles.
Fitting. Nothing gets up there without wings.
So you don't attack.
You send your people in first, quietly, one at a time.
They take jobs. They make friends. They convert the soldiers.
The story goes that you slip in yourself, disguised as a schoolteacher.
Then, in 1090, the castle simply belongs to you.
Its lord, a man named Mahdi, is shown the door.
One tradition says you even pay him.
A note for three thousand gold dinars, to be cashed by a Seljuk official.
You stole a castle, and sent the bill to the enemy.
Not one battle.
Quick pause.
A lot of you asked for an assassin, so here's where the real ones began.
Who should live next? Leave a name in the comments.
And if you want a new life every day, subscribe.
The most powerful man in the Seljuk empire is not the sultan.
It's his grand vizier, Nizam al-Mulk.
He's run the empire for nearly thirty years.
And he wants your movement wiped out.
October 1092. Near Nahavand.
The old vizier is carried in his litter after a meal.
A man dressed as a Sufi holy man walks up with a petition.
Then a knife.
Nizam al-Mulk is dead.
A few weeks later, Sultan Malik-Shah dies too.
Most chroniclers blame you. Nobody agrees on who really gave the order.
But the empire learns a new kind of fear.
Your fighters are called fidai. The ones who give themselves.
One man. One blade. No escape planned.
And no army can stop that.
There's an old legend that you, Nizam, and the poet Omar Khayyam were schoolboys together.
That you swore a pact to help each other.
It's a great story. Historians say it never happened.
In 1094, the caliph in Cairo dies.
His elder son Nizar was supposed to be next.
But Badr's son, now vizier himself, puts the younger brother on the throne instead.
Remember Cairo?
It just chose against you, again.
Nizar is thrown into prison, and dies there in 1095.
So you make the biggest decision of your life.
You break with Cairo. You stay loyal to Nizar's line.
From now on, your people are the Nizaris.
And you answer to no one on Earth.
You never leave Alamut again.
The chroniclers say you spend thirty-four years in the castle, mostly in your room.
Reading. Writing. Praying.
Remember the books?
You build a library on top of a mountain.
Books, instruments, star charts, hauled up by hand.
Down below, your people cut channels into the rock and terrace the slopes.
Water cisterns. Grain stores. Fields of barley.
The castle can feed itself for years.
Remember how you learned to wait?
Seljuk armies come up the valley again and again.
In 1109, the biggest one yet.
You wait. It fails.
Your rules are total. No wine. No exceptions.
Not even for family.
One son is accused of murder. The other is suspected of drinking wine.
You have them both executed.
Your wife and daughters are sent to another fortress, Girdkuh.
There they spin wool for a living.
You run a kingdom of castles, and your own house is empty.
And the legend of the dagger?
The historian Juvayni says Sultan Sanjar wakes one morning to find a knife stuck in the ground beside his bed.
With a note from Alamut.
Sanjar makes peace.
It's 1124. You're in your seventies.
Your movement holds castles across Persia, with followers as far as Syria.
In the spring, you fall ill.
Remember the fever that made you who you are?
This time, there's no getting up.
You name your successor, Buzurg-Ummid, a commander you trust.
And in June 1124, in Alamut, you die.
You're buried near the rock you never came down from.
The castles you built hold on for more than a century.
Then, in 1256, the Mongols arrive.
Alamut surrenders, and is torn down.
The historian Juvayni walks through your library.
He takes a few books, and burns the rest.
Later, Europeans fill the gap with legends.
Marco Polo writes about a secret garden, and young killers drugged into obedience.
Modern historians call it fantasy.
Enemies called your people hashishin. An insult.
In Europe it becomes a word: assassin.
And the famous line, nothing is true, everything is permitted? You almost certainly never said it.
You lost both sons, by your own order.
You sent away your wife and daughters.
You gave up the whole world for one room on a rock.
You took a fortress without a battle.
You frightened an empire with a handful of men.
And an insult for your people became a word every language knows.
So tell me.
Was Hassan-i Sabbah a holy man protecting his people, or the first master of terror?
